title: This Shouldn’t be such a Fringe Idea
author: Ruth Poulsen
summary: Ruth Poulsen argues that schools should adopt a digital sunset: a school-wide agreement not to send emails or work texts after 6 pm, at weekends or in holidays, using schedule-send for anything written outside those hours. She links the always-on infinite workday to poor mental health among school leaders, citing a study in which work spillage into home life was the only predictor of principals' depression and anxiety. Drawing on the Nagoskis' Burnout, she explains that the nervous system cannot tell an angry email from a predator, so stress hormones linger unless the stress cycle is physically completed. Having implemented digital sunsets in three schools, she lists the supporting systems that make them work, including a 24-hour response norm, shared meeting agendas and in-person handling of emotionally loaded conversations. She closes with steps for teachers who lack authority over school-wide norms.
points: A digital sunset removes after-hours email and work texts as a shared norm, so staff are not interrupted at dinner or bedtime and individuals can still work late using schedule-send.
Poulsen cites research on principals finding that work spillage, meaning emails and tasks taken home, was the only thing that predicted poor mental health.
The biological argument is that notifications keep the sympathetic nervous system active, so safety must be felt in the body rather than reasoned into place.
The policy needs supports: a stated response window counting only work days, shared meeting agendas, in-person talk for complex issues, and no late-night collaborative document comments.
Teachers without authority can share the article with a principal, agree a bubble with close colleagues, or add friction to their own phone notifications.
quotes: A digital sunset is a school-wide agreement that we don’t send each other emails or work texts after 6 pm, on weekends, or during holidays. If you want to go home, be with your kids or walk your dog and then log back on and work in the evening, go right ahead– but use schedule-send for anything you’re sharing with others.
But there used to be a meaningful barrier between being online and real life. Now, our online lives—including our email inboxes— seep into every nook and cranny of our day.

Just as regenerative farmers plan a crop rotation of grains and pastures to allow their soil to rest and regain its fertility, regenerative school leaders intentionally protect cycles of rest and work for themselves and their teachers.
Crucially, your nervous system can’t tell the difference between a predator and an angry email: either one activates your sympathetic nervous system.
Telling yourself It’s the weekend, stop being stressed! is like telling your stomach to stop digesting a heavy meal. You actually have to do something to let your body know that you are safe.

I’ve implemented digital sunset agreements in three schools now. In general, I try to be the kind of administrator who doesn’t have any “suitcase initiatives:” policies and programs that I bring with me to each new school regardless of context.
Deliberately putting up barriers to interrupt the infinite workday is a practical way to show real care to your staff.
We don’t have to model the infinite workday for our students, inculcating them into a world where burnout is just so normal.
context: The policy is defined as a shared norm rather than a personal rule of restraint.
Constant availability has replaced the old boundary between work and home.
The farming metaphor casts rest as a planned part of sustaining staff.
Notifications trigger a physical stress response that willpower cannot switch off.
Stress ends through bodily safety signals, not by telling yourself to relax.
Poulsen advocates this policy in every school, unlike most initiatives she carries.
Removing after-hours email is framed as concrete care for staff.
Students learn burnout norms from the adults who model the infinite workday.
